name: Building AI Agents
objectives: In a Colab notebook, write two tools as Python functions with clear names, one-line descriptions and input checks, each tool working when you call it yourself
Given your tools and a goal, write a system prompt and an ask_model helper that make the model reply with one action in JSON, so the model picks a valid tool or a final answer
Given the model's chosen action, write a loop that runs the chosen tool and feeds the result back to the model, until the model gives a final answer
While the agent runs, keep the history tidy and record every step in a run log, with step, raw reply, tool, input and result for each step
Given a bad model reply, a tool error or a long run, add a step limit and handle bad replies and tool errors, so the agent recovers or stops and reports without crashing
Given your finished agent, test it on normal and impossible goals and explain when a framework would help, running all five tests and writing what you fixed

chapters.name: Chapter 1: The agent loop in code

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Tools are just functions
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write two tools as Python functions with clear names and descriptions.
This lesson builds toward: In a Colab notebook, you will write two tools as Python functions with clear names, one-line descriptions and input checks, each tool working when you call it yourself.
To an agent, a tool is a function your code runs when the model asks. The model never runs anything itself: it only writes the name of a tool and its input. Your code decides whether to run it.
Start with safe, read-only tools. A calculator: def calculator(expression): with a body that only allows digits and + - * / ( ) . and then works out the answer. A notes lookup: NOTES = {'schedule': 'Class days: Mon, Wed, Thu'}, and def lookup_note(topic): return NOTES.get(topic, 'no note found').
Collect them in a dictionary so the loop can find them by name: TOOLS = {'calculator': calculator, 'lookup_note': lookup_note}. Write a one-line description for each. The model reads those descriptions to choose, so they matter as much as the code.
Step by step:
- Write each tool as a Python function with one input.
- Make it safe: check the input before using it.
- Return text the model can read, including a clear message on failure.
- Put the tools in a TOOLS dictionary.
- Write a one-line description of each tool.
Words to know:
- Function: a named block of code that takes input and returns a result.
- Dictionary: a Python collection of name and value pairs, like {'calculator': calculator}.
- Read-only tool: a tool that only looks things up and changes nothing.
Try it now: In a new Colab notebook, write calculator and lookup_note, put them in TOOLS, and test each by calling it yourself: calculator('45*12/60') and lookup_note('schedule').
You can now write safe tools as Python functions and register them by name.

check.q: In your agent, what is a tool?
options: A Python function your code runs when the model asks
A website the model visits on its own
check.why: The model only asks; your code runs the function.

check.q: Your lookup_note tool gets a topic that is not in the notes. What should it do?
options: Return a clear message that the topic was not found
check.why: A clear message lets the model try something else instead of guessing.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Asking the model for its next action
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a prompt that makes the model reply with one action in JSON.
This lesson builds toward: Given your tools and a goal, you will write a system prompt and an ask_model helper that make the model reply with one action in JSON, so the model picks a valid tool or a final answer.
The model needs to know the goal, the tools and the reply format. Your system prompt lists each tool with its description and says: reply with only JSON, either {"tool": "name", "input": "..."} to use a tool, or {"final": "..."} when the goal is met.
Add rules from your design card: use only the listed tools; one action per reply; if a tool result says it failed, try a different approach; never invent a tool result.
Write a helper so the rest of your code does not care which provider you use: def ask_model(text): that calls your model (copy the call from your provider's quickstart, as in course 2) and returns the answer text. If you change providers later, only ask_model changes.
Step by step:
- List each tool name and its description in the system prompt.
- Give the two JSON reply shapes: tool or final.
- Add the rules from your design card.
- Write ask_model(text) that returns the model's answer text.
- Test it once with the goal and print the reply.
Words to know:
- Action: one thing the agent decides to do next, like using a tool or giving the final answer.
- Helper function: a small function that hides details, like which model provider you call.
Try it now: Write the system prompt and ask_model. Send the goal from the final task and print the reply. Did it choose lookup_note first? If not, improve the tool descriptions.
You can now get a model to choose its next action as JSON from a list of tools.

check.q: What should the model's reply look like when it wants a tool?
options: A friendly paragraph explaining its plan
One JSON action that names the tool and its input
The Python code for the tool
check.why: One JSON action is something your loop can read and run.

check.q: The model keeps choosing the calculator before it has the class days. What would you change first?
options: Improve the tool descriptions so it knows to look up notes first
check.why: The model chooses tools from their descriptions, so clearer descriptions guide its choice.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Running the loop: act and feed back
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write the loop that runs the chosen tool and feeds the result back.
This lesson builds toward: Given the model's chosen action, you will write a loop that runs the chosen tool and feeds the result back to the model, until the model gives a final answer.
The loop is short. history = [] holds what happened. For each step: build the text (system prompt, goal, history), call ask_model, parse the JSON. If it has 'final', print it and stop. If it has 'tool', look it up in TOOLS, run it with the input, and add a line to history: the action and the result.
Feeding back the result is the observe step from course 1. Without it the model would ask for the same thing forever. With it, the model sees "lookup_note(schedule) returned: Class days: Mon, Wed, Thu" and can decide the next step, such as using the calculator.
If the model names a tool that is not in TOOLS, do not crash: add "Unknown tool: X. Use one of: calculator, lookup_note" to the history and continue. Clear messages back to the model are how an agent recovers from its own mistakes.
Step by step:
- history = []
- Build the text: system prompt, goal, history.
- Call ask_model and parse the JSON.
- If 'final': print and stop.
- If 'tool': run it from TOOLS and add the action and result to history.
Words to know:
- History: the running list of actions and results the agent has seen this run.
- Observation: the result of a tool, fed back to the model.
Try it now: Write the loop and run it on the final-task goal. Print history after each step. Count how many steps it took to reach a final answer.
You can now write an agent loop that runs tools and feeds the results back to the model.

check.q: What is the observe step in the loop?
options: Adding the tool result to the history so the model sees it
check.why: Feeding the result back lets the model decide its next step from what happened.

check.q: Your agent calls the same tool again and again. What is the most likely fix?
options: Make sure each tool result is fed back into the history
check.why: Without the result in history, the model does not know the action already ran.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Memory and a run log
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Keep short-term memory tidy and log every step.
This lesson builds toward: While the agent runs, you will keep the history tidy and record every step in a run log, with step, raw reply, tool, input and result for each step.
Short-term memory is the history list you already have. It grows every step, and everything in it is sent to the model, which costs tokens and time. For long runs, keep the last few steps in full and replace older steps with a one-line summary.
Long-term memory is anything saved between runs: a notes file, a spreadsheet, a small database. Save only what the agent truly needs next time, and never save private data you do not need.
A run log is for you, not the model. For each step, record the step number, the model's raw reply, the tool and input, the result and the time. When the agent does something odd, the log tells you why. A simple way: log.append({'step': n, 'reply': reply, 'result': result}) and print it at the end.
Words to know:
- Short-term memory: what the agent sees during one run: the history so far.
- Long-term memory: information saved between runs, such as a notes file.
- Run log: your record of every step the agent took, for checking and debugging.
Try it now: Add a log list to your agent and record each step. Run it, then print the log as a neat table: step, tool, input, result.
You can now manage an agent's memory and keep a run log you can read.

check.q: What is short-term memory in your agent?
options: The history list for this run
check.why: Short-term memory is the history the agent keeps during one run.

check.q: The agent gave a strange answer and you want to know why. What do you look at?
options: The run log of every step
check.why: The log shows each reply, tool, input and result, so you can see where it went wrong.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Step limits, bad replies and errors
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Add a step limit and handle bad model replies and tool errors.
This lesson builds toward: Given a bad model reply, a tool error or a long run, you will add a step limit and handle bad replies and tool errors, so the agent recovers or stops and reports without crashing.
Every loop needs a ceiling: MAX_STEPS = 6 and for step in range(MAX_STEPS): instead of a loop that runs forever. If it reaches the limit without a final answer, stop and report "Stopped: step limit reached" with the log.
Bad replies happen: extra words around the JSON, a missing key, an empty answer. Parse inside try and except. On failure, add "Your last reply was not valid JSON. Reply with only JSON." to history and let the next step try again. Count these; if there are two in a row, stop.
Tools fail too: a calculator gets letters, a file is missing. Each tool should catch its own errors and return a clear message such as "calculator error: only numbers and + - * / allowed". The model can then fix its input on the next step.
Step by step:
- Set MAX_STEPS and loop with range(MAX_STEPS).
- Parse replies inside try / except.
- On a bad reply, tell the model and continue.
- Stop after two bad replies in a row.
- Make every tool return a clear error message instead of crashing.
Words to know:
- Step limit: the most steps an agent may take in one run.
- Exception: an error that happens while a program runs; try / except catches it.
Try it now: Test your safety code: temporarily make ask_model return "hello" on step 2, and send calculator the input 'abc'. Check the agent recovers, and that it stops at the step limit when you set MAX_STEPS = 2.
You can now keep an agent from looping forever and help it recover from bad replies and tool errors.

options: Sets a ceiling on how many steps the agent can take
Limits how many tools you can write
Sets how long the log can be
check.why: A step limit stops a run that would otherwise go on and on.

check.q: The model replies "hello" instead of JSON on one step. What should your agent do?
options: Tell the model to reply with only JSON and continue
Start the whole run again from step 1
check.why: One bad reply can be recovered; the agent stops only after repeated bad replies.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Frameworks, and finishing your first agent
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Finish and test your agent, and know when a framework would help.
This lesson builds toward: Given your finished agent, you will test it on normal and impossible goals and explain when a framework would help, running all five tests and writing what you fixed.
Agent frameworks are libraries that give you the loop, tool handling and memory ready-made. Well-known ones include LangGraph, CrewAI, the OpenAI Agents SDK and Google's Agent Development Kit, and many model providers support native tool calling, where the model returns a structured tool call for you. They change often, so read each project's own documentation for current setup.
Building the loop yourself first means you understand what a framework does for you, and you can debug it when it goes wrong. Many real agents are still a plain loop like yours.
Before you call your agent done, test it like course 2: three goals it should finish, one it cannot (it should say so, not invent an answer), and one bad input. Read the log for each run.
Step by step:
- Run the agent on three goals it should finish.
- Run one goal it cannot finish: it should say so.
- Run one bad input.
- Read the log for each run.
- Fix one weakness and rerun all five.
Words to know:
- Framework: a ready-made library that handles common parts of a program for you.
- Native tool calling: a model feature where the model returns a structured request to use a tool.
Try it now: Final task: finish your two-tool agent on the study-hours goal with a 6-step limit, one recovered bad reply and a printed log of every step. Then run the five tests above and write two sentences on what you fixed.
You can now build, test and explain a working AI agent in plain Python.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Two working tools A tool is missing, crashes, or has no description. Both tools work, have clear names and descriptions, and check their input. Tools return clear error messages the model can act on. Actions in JSON The model replies in free text the loop cannot read. The model chooses tools and a final answer in JSON. The prompt also tells the model never to invent a tool result. Loop feeds results back Tool results are not fed back, or the loop never ends. The loop runs the chosen tool, feeds the result back and stops at a final answer. Unknown tool names are handled by telling the model which tools exist. Safety limits No step limit, or a bad reply crashes the agent. Stops at a 6-step limit and recovers from one bad model reply. Also handles a tool error and stops after two bad replies in a row. Run log No log, or steps are missing from it. Prints a log of every step. The log is a neat table someone else could read to explain the run. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: A ready-made loop, tools and memory you can use instead of writing your own
check.why: Frameworks package the parts you built by hand in this course.

check.q: You give your agent a goal it cannot reach with its tools. What should a good agent do?
options: Say it cannot finish and show what it tried
Invent an answer that sounds right
Call a tool that does not exist
check.why: An honest agent reports what it could not do instead of making something up.
